leads.name: Zwarte populier Noorderplantsoen Groningen
leads.species: Black Poplar (Populus nigra), possibly common poplar per register's own doubt
leads.reason: Register (netherlands-lrmb nr 1680853) calls this the tallest/thickest tree in Noorderplantsoen ('de koning van het plantsoen') but its own 2020 note records large sections of dying bark and says the tree is entering its final phase, though still alive with enough sap flow for lush foliage as of the register's last update. It also sits only 31.2 m from the already-published gro_004 (The Duck's Foot Tree of Noorderplantsoen, Ginkgo biloba) per the brief's near_published flag, a different species but close enough that a health recheck and a clearer sense of it as its own distinct stop (not just 'more park trees near the ginkgo') should happen before it ships. Not blocked: nothing here says it is dead, and a declining-but-alive veteran is exactly the kind of tree this project wants once its status is current.

leads.name: Valse acacia (Zuiderpark 2)
leads.reason: Register lists this tree at the same address, 'Zuiderpark 2, Groningen', as the already-blocked Plataan (villa front garden, visitable 'nee'), but WITHOUT the 'voortuin villa' qualifier, with owner_category 'gemeente' (not the villa's private ownership) and visitable 'ja'. Web search confirms Zuiderpark is a villa neighbourhood laid out as a municipal public park (plantsoen) in 1883 by the gemeente, and that robinia is among the species the park itself contains, so a gemeente-owned, visitable robinia at this street frontage is plausible as a public-park tree distinct from the villa's own front garden. But the coordinate is identical to the private villa's, and no source found this pass distinguishes 'stands in the public plantsoen strip' from 'stands in the villa's front garden' for this specific specimen. Left as a lead rather than shipped: a future pass should check aerial imagery or a street-level photo to see whether this tree sits on the public park side of the property line or inside the villa's grounds.

leads.reason: Register's own place field: 'Park nabij Oosterhaven, Groningen. The register itself records that even the municipality could not pin down this tree's location as of 2015, which is a stronger problem than ordinary approximate precision: it puts the tree's continued existence and location both in doubt from the source's own words, and no second source (news, local history, a park inventory) was found this pass to confirm it. leads.name: Grauwe abeel (Bloemsingel/Bloemstraat)
leads.reason: Register (nr 1680047) lists this tree at 'Bloemsingel, kruising Bloemstraat', owner_category 'publiekrechtelijke organisatie' (a public body, not a private individual, unlike the villa lead below) and visitable 'ja'. Distinct from the already-blocked 'Gewone plataan RUG / Hollandse iep' pair (Bloemstraat 36 binnenplaats, ~130m away): that pair sits inside a specific faculty building's inner courtyard, this one is registered at the street intersection itself. This pass found Bloemsingel 1 is a large 1911 educational building (6,078 sqm, 'onderwijsfunctie') right at that corner, but found no source confirming whether the tree stands on open street/plantsoen ground at the intersection or inside that institution's own grounds. Register's 'ja' for visitable is a real signal but not, on its own, the same as a source describing what a visitor would actually meet there. Left as a lead pending either a site-level source (satellite/street view check, or a Groningen tree-inventory record with an exact address) or a future pass with time to look.

leads.name: The Siberian Balsam Poplar of Engelenpoortje

location.address: Engelenpoortje, between Poelestraat and Nieuwe Markt, Groningen

leads.story:
This poplar is not a species anyone would find growing wild anywhere. Populus x berolinensis was bred in 1865 in Berlin's botanical garden, a deliberate cross between a Siberian laurel-leaf poplar and the tall, narrow Lombardy poplar, made for exactly the trait it shows here, height with a narrow enough crown to survive in a gap between buildings barely wider than the tree itself.

It grows at the Engelenpoortje, a seventeenth-century gated alley named for a long-vanished inn, De Blauwe Engel, that once stood on the corner. The alley has not had a settled recent history: redevelopment around Groningen's Grote Markt closed it to the public in 2012, and it stayed shut for eight years before reopening at the end of 2020. Whether this poplar, which the register dates to the 1930s, stood through that closure without anyone walking past it is not recorded, though a cross this vigorous would have lost little from eight quiet years. It stands today between the shops and houses the alley threads between, free to walk past on the way from Poelestraat to the Nieuwe Markt, exactly as the seventeenth-century gate always intended.
leads.access: Free, public alley, open at any time
leads.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its tall, narrow crown, bred to fit into a gap between buildings barely wider than the tree itself. It stands in the Engelenpoortje alley, between Poelestraat and Nieuwe Markt.
leads.removed_reason: Dead or felled per the register itself: Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen nr 1680039 carries status 5, Dood/geveld (checked 2026-10-10 against the Bomenstichting ArcGIS layer). Removed under the rule that a dead tree is never a collectible entry.

leads.name: The Chestnut of Prinsentuin
leads.story:
The Prinsentuin has been walled off from the rest of Groningen since 1626, when it was laid out as a private pleasure garden for the region's stadholders, and the wall is still what makes it feel like a secret in the middle of a busy city centre. Visitors reach it through a gate on the Turfsingel topped with a working sundial from 1731, accurate enough to mark day length and sunrise and sunset as well as the hour, or through a smaller door on Kattenhage. Entry is free and has been for as long as records go back.

This horse chestnut, which the tree register dates to around 1850 to 1860, is not part of the garden's original seventeenth-century planting, arriving roughly two centuries after the walls went up, but it has still had well over 150 years inside them. Horse chestnut is not native to the Netherlands, imported from the Balkans as an ornamental tree from the sixteenth century onward, and this one has grown up sheltered from wind and street salt by walls built for a stadholder's roses rather than for any tree. It stands in the open garden, free, daily until sunset, a short walk from Martinikerkhof.
leads.access: Free, public walled garden, open daily until sunset
leads.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station

photo.attribution: The original uploader was Fruggo at Dutch Wikipedia, via Wikimedia Commons

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by growing inside the walled Prinsentuin garden, reached through the gate topped with a working 1731 sundial. It stands in the Prinsentuin, entrance on Turfsingel.

leads.name: The Chestnut of Akerkhof

location.address: Akerkhof, around the Akerk church, Groningen

leads.story:
When Groningen redeveloped the Akerkhof a few years ago to fix a square that had gone dark, dry and unloved, the plan called for cutting three trees and clearing scrub around the church to let light back in. This horse chestnut was not one of them. The municipality's own account of the project says its monumental chestnut and linden trees deliberately kept their place and gained more room as the work went on, while three new trees were planted along the redesigned Brugstraat to make up for what came down.

Akerkhof was a real cemetery from the twelfth century until burials inside the city walls were banned on hygiene grounds and the ground was cleared in 1828, which is most of why an open square with old trees exists here at all. This chestnut, dated by the register to around 1880 to 1890, is younger than that clearance but has still stood through the square's dark spell and its recent recovery. It grows in the open around the Akerk church, free to walk past any time, on a square the city now treats as worth protecting rather than merely tolerating.
leads.access: Free, public square, open at any time
leads.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 12 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station
leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the extra room deliberately cleared around it during the square's recent redevelopment. It stands in the open around the Akerk church on Akerkhof.

leads.name: The Maple of Guyotplein
leads.story:
This sycamore grows on a square named for a man most Dutch schoolchildren have never heard of, Henri Daniel Guyot, a Walloon minister who founded the country's first school for deaf children in Groningen in 1790. The square itself started as the planted west side of the Ossenmarkt, given trees in 1754, and only took Guyot's name in 1890, on the centenary of his institute, by which point this specific tree, dated by the register to around 1890 to 1900, was likely just going into the ground.

A monument to Guyot has stood on the square since 1829, decades before it carried his name, and the deaf institute itself operated here for generations before the building later became Groningen's courthouse. The sycamore has outlasted the institute's departure and watched the square's slow shift from an educational address to a judicial one. Sycamore sheds bark in flaking plates as it ages, closer to a plane tree's trunk than to most other maples, worth a look on this one after more than a century of growth. It stands in the open square, free, a short walk from the city's other historic squares.
leads.access: Free, public square, open at any time
leads.transport: Binnenstad, central Groningen; about a 10 minute walk from Groningen Centraal station

best_time.label: September to October: winged seeds that spin down in pairs

leads.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its bark shedding in flaking plates like a plane tree's, unusual among maples. It stands on Guyotplein, beside the 1829 monument to Henri Daniel Guyot.

blocked.name: Gewone plataan RUG / Hollandse iep (pair, adjacent coordinates)
blocked.species: London Plane (Platanus x acerifolia) and Dutch Elm
blocked.reason: Checked 2026-08-23 (the school/campus access test this lead was waiting on). Register's own 'place' field for both trees reads 'Bloemstraat 36 (binnenplaats)', i.e. the inner courtyard of a specific address rather than open campus grounds. A web search identifies Bloemstraat 36 as the University of Groningen's Faculty of Behavioural and Social Sciences building (built 1975, faculty office building 4122-4123), not a public quad or park; nothing found describes its courtyard as open to visitors. The register itself lists 'visitable: onbekend' (unknown) for both trees, and 'visible: onbekend' for the elm specifically (only the plane is marked visible). The elm additionally carries owner_category 'particulier' (private party), unusual for a spot described as university terrain, and its status code (5) differs from the plane's (3), suggesting the register itself treats the two entries differently. No source found this pass confirms a member of the public can walk into this courtyard without a reason to be in the building. Fails the 'can they get in without asking anyone's permission' test in hard rule 10; blocked rather than shipped as approximate. Matches the pattern already established for this city's other binnenplaats entries below (Turfsingel beech and walnut).

blocked.name: Witte paardenkastanje Pelstergasthuis Groningen
blocked.reason: Register's own history ends: 'En toen viel de boom spontaan om! Zie laatste waarneming' (and then the tree spontaneously fell over! see latest observation), following a multi-year record of a bracket-fungus infection (dikrand tondelzwam, korstjeshoutskoolzwam) at the trunk base. Dead/fallen, confirmed by the register's own last entry. Blocked, we doen niet aan dode bomen. Also note: even before falling, it stood 'in het hofje... tegen de gevel geklemd' (clamped against the facade in the hofje courtyard), so it would also have needed an access check.

blocked.name: Plataan park Hereweg / Zuiderpark 2 villa
blocked.reason: Register's own place field: 'Zuiderpark 2 (voortuin villa)', i.e. the front garden of a specific villa, not the public Zuiderpark despite the street name. Confirmed by web search: Zuiderpark 2 is a protected Rijksmonument villa built 1881/82 for R.P. Cleveringa, 'currently still in use as a residence' (monumenten.nl/rijksmonumenten.nl). The register itself records visitable as 'nee' (visible 'ja', i.e. glimpsable but not enterable). A private residence's front garden is excluded under hard rule 10 (front gardens and private houses stay out whatever the register says), whatever partial street-level visibility exists. Blocked rather than shipped as a view-only tree, because view-only ships only when the source affirmatively describes public visibility, not merely 'visible: ja' against a 'visitable: nee' private-residence flag.

blocked.name: Witte paardenkastanje (Munnikeholm/Schoolholm binnentuin)
blocked.reason: Register's own 'place' field: 'In binnentuin tussen Munnikeholm en Schoolholm, Groningen. Is gekapt in sept 2010. Kastanjeziekte 2015 CE.' The register's own text records the tree as felled ('gekapt') in September 2010, with a further note about chestnut disease dated 2015 (possibly referring to a resprout or a neighbouring tree, unclear, but the felling statement is unambiguous). Web search for the inner courtyard between these two streets found only unrelated general descriptions of the area's courtyards, nothing contradicting the felling. Blocked as dead/removed per the register's own history, matching the pattern of this city's other already-blocked chestnut (Pelstergasthuis, 'toen viel de boom spontaan om').
